passage: Vasudha had skipped three birthday parties this year. Each time, as soon as Mummy said, "Fine, stay home," the tightness in her chest melted. It felt wonderful. And the next invitation felt even scarier. Now it was Nazia's sleepover, and it was pouring. "What if I can't sleep? What if I cry and everyone sees?" Mummy sat on the bed. "Let's try a smaller step. Go for dinner and the film. I'll pick you up at nine." "But it's raining. What if you can't come?" "Then I'll come late, with the big umbrella. I will come." At nine, Mummy was at Nazia's door, soaked to the knees. Vasudha ran out, glowing. "We made pizza! Next time, maybe I'll stay till ten."

qa.q: What time did Mummy promise to pick Vasudha up?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel each time she was allowed to skip a party?
qa.a: She felt relief as the tightness in her chest melted, but the next invitation felt even scarier.

qa.q: What small step helped Vasudha face the sleepover?
qa.a: Going just for dinner and the film, with a firm promise of a nine o'clock pickup, even in the rain.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel about Vasudha coming, even for part of the evening?
qa.a: Nazia would likely be glad Vasudha came and made pizza, instead of missing her again.

grounding: It shows a child who avoids parties and sleepovers out of fear and feels relief when excused, and a smaller, supported step that is wiser than avoiding.

passage: On the morning of the science exam, Disha woke with a pounding head and begged to stay home from her Pune school. Last term she had missed two exams the same way, and each time, once she was allowed to stay home, she felt instantly better. This time her mother phoned the school counsellor, Rehana Ma'am, first. "Let her come," Rehana said. "She can write the paper in the small room next to my office, with only one other student. We'll build up to the big hall." Disha sat in the small room with her hands shaking. Rehana Ma'am smiled through the glass door, and Disha wrote the first answer, then the next. Two weeks later, for the maths paper, Disha sat in the big hall, near the door.

qa.q: Where did Disha write the science paper?
qa.a: In the small room next to the counsellor's office, with only one other student.

qa.q: Why did Disha feel better whenever she stayed home from an exam?
qa.a: Staying home took away the frightening situation, so she felt instant relief.

qa.q: What was the key choice that changed the pattern?
qa.a: Instead of letting Disha stay home again, her mother and the counsellor gave her a smaller, supported step toward the exam.

qa.q: How might Disha's mother feel watching her sit the maths paper in the big hall?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and relieved that the small steps worked instead of the avoidance growing.

grounding: It shows a child who avoids exam days and feels relief when excused, and a counsellor and parent who plan supportive small exposures instead.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Valentina, ten, was invited to her cousin Santiago's birthday sleepover. Her stomach dropped. What if she couldn't sleep? What if she cried in front of everyone? She begged her mother to say she was ill, and when her mother agreed, Valentina felt a huge rush of relief. But the next month she refused a school trip too, and then a friend's afternoon party. Her mother saw the pattern. "Every time we say no, the fear gets bigger. What if you go to Santiago's until nine and I pick you up?" Valentina was scared but agreed. At nine she was laughing so hard over a card game she asked, "Can I stay till ten?"

qa.q: What did Valentina's mother suggest as a first step?
qa.a: She suggested Valentina go to Santiago's until nine and be picked up.

qa.q: How did Valentina feel when she was excused from the sleepover?
qa.a: She felt a huge rush of relief, but that relief made her avoid more things afterwards.

qa.q: Why was the "until nine" plan wiser than staying home?
qa.a: It was a small, supported step toward the fear, so the fear could shrink instead of growing with each avoidance.

qa.q: How might Santiago feel when Valentina asks to stay till ten?
qa.a: He may feel happy that his cousin is enjoying his party and wants to stay longer.

grounding: Shows a child who avoids a sleepover and feels relief when excused, the avoidance growing, and a supportive small step that helps.

passage: On the morning of the maths test, Mahima, eleven, was in the school sick room again, clutching her stomach. Gopika, the school nurse, checked her gently; she had been there on the last three test days. Every time she was sent home, Mahima's shoulders dropped with relief. Gopika sat beside her. "When you miss tests, does the fear get smaller or bigger next time?" Mahima whispered, "Bigger." Gopika phoned her parents and spoke to her class teacher that same morning. The plan: Mahima would sit the first half of today's test in the quiet room next to the office, with a glass of water, and then decide. She finished the whole paper. "It was hard," she said, "but I did it."

qa.q: Where did Mahima sit the test?
qa.a: She sat it in the quiet room next to the office.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel whenever she was sent home on test days?
qa.a: She felt relief, her shoulders dropping, but the fear grew bigger each time.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that was wise?
qa.a: She gently helped Mahima notice the avoidance pattern, involved her parents and teacher, and set up a small, supported step to face the test.

qa.q: How might Mahima's class teacher see her after she finished the paper?
qa.a: The teacher may see her as braver and more capable than her sick-room visits suggested.

grounding: Shows a child avoiding exam days and relieved when excused, with the relief feeding avoidance, and a nurse arranging a supported small step instead.

passage:
Saturday: Dilnaz, nine, refused to go to Usha Aunty's daughter's birthday party. "Too many people. What if I get lost?" Ammi let her stay home, and Dilnaz felt light with relief. But on Monday she refused the school picnic too.
Wednesday: Ammi called Usha Aunty. "She gets scared in crowds. Could she come early to help set up, before everyone arrives, for the next party?" Usha laughed kindly. "Rimi's other birthday party is at her grandmother's on Sunday. Come at four."
Sunday: Dilnaz arrived at four, blew up twelve balloons and hung streamers with Rimi. When the guests came, she already knew every corner of the room. She stayed until the cake, and then until the games.

qa.q: How many balloons did Dilnaz blow up?
qa.a: She blew up twelve balloons.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when Ammi let her skip the first party?
qa.a: She felt light with relief, but then she refused the school picnic too, so the fear was spreading.

qa.q: What small step helped Dilnaz go to the party?
qa.a: Arriving early to help set up before guests came, so the room felt familiar and safe.

qa.q: How might Usha Aunty feel seeing Dilnaz stay until the games?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and warm that her small help made the party possible for Dilnaz.

grounding: Shows a child whose avoidance of parties brings relief and spreads, and how a supportive small step helps her take part.

passage:
So you don't want to go to Aarav's sleepover, Eshaan? Let me tell you about my little brother Deepu, when he was nine. Your Sharmila Dadi remembers this well.
Deepu got invited to a cousin's birthday. His stomach hurt the night before. Our mother said, "Stay home then." He was so relieved he was smiling by dinner.
But next time, a school trip, he said no faster. Then the annual exam; he cried that he couldn't go. Each time he was let off, the fear grew bigger, like a dog you keep feeding.
Our father saw it. He didn't force him. He said, "Just come to the party for thirty minutes. I'll wait outside." Deepu went, shaking. He stayed forty.
Next time, one hour. By the end of that year, he went on the school trip. So, Eshaan, what if you go for dinner and come home before bed?

qa.q: How long did Deepu stay at the party the first time?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Deepu feel when he was allowed to stay home from the birthday?
qa.a: He felt relieved and happy, smiling by dinner, even though that relief made the fear grow later.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Deepu's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: His father offered a short, supported visit with him waiting outside; small, safe steps showed Deepu he could cope instead of avoiding.

qa.q: How might Deepu's father have felt watching the fear grow?
qa.a: He was probably worried, but calm and trusting enough to help Deepu face it gently.

grounding: Sharmila Dadi tells Eshaan how her brother's fear grew each time he was excused, until supportive small exposures helped him.
